props.covers: The layout agent's tool surface and the edit it serves: how one scoped AI-driven canvas edit moves from operator instruction to a validated cumulative proposal, why the thirty-two tools are factored by editing gesture rather than by CRUD per kind, the full roster, the calls the surface absorbs, and the scope it deliberately excludes.

text.insert: An edit starts when the operator selects canvas objects and tells the studio what should change. The harness resolves that scope, opens a draft from the current document, and gives the model a complete textual and visual starting point. The model edits the draft directly through validated, id-addressed operations.

Each applied operation returns a focused account of its effect and re-renders the draft, so the standing picture (digest, cumulative diff, findings, and a render of the board as it stands) rides the state block into the next turn. look is the deliberate close-up on one region on top of it. The saved board is not changed until a cumulative proposal passes the run gates and the operator accepts it.
One edit, in order

The studio owns the operator-facing session. The harness owns the baseline, scope, draft, request queue, and tool runtime. The model supplies layout judgment, and every picture it judges from (the board render riding each state block and the region look frames) comes from the canvas renderer, so the model reads the same routed visual truth the product draws.

props.caption: The model edits a session draft through typed single-operation tools, judges the whole board from the render riding each state block, and spends look on one framed region at a time; finalize proposes the cumulative baseline-to-draft diff.
props.title: One scoped edit, from instruction to proposal

text.insert:
sequenceDiagram
  participant Studio as Operator / Studio
  participant Harness as Harness session
  participant Model
  participant Renderer as Canvas renderer
  Studio->>Harness: select objects, instruct, create session
  Harness->>Harness: resolve scope, copy baseline, inject page frame, sync requests
  Harness->>Renderer: renderBoardView(current draft)
  Renderer-->>Harness: full-board PNG
  Harness-->>Model: five context blocks + board image + exemplar + vocabulary sheet
  loop study, edit, and review
    Harness-->>Model: state block: BOARD + BOARD DIFF + DIAGNOSTICS + REQUESTS + the board as it stands
    Model->>Harness: one typed gesture({ operation fields })
    Harness->>Harness: snap geometry to the 20 grid, validate one operation
    alt operation applies
      Harness->>Harness: apply, reconcile membership and waypoints, commit the draft, re-render, diff, lint
      Harness-->>Model: APPLIED + notes + DELTA + lint delta + ROUTES
    else legal operation has nothing to do
      Harness-->>Model: NO-OP + note (edge gestures still return the fresh polyline)
    else state validation fails
      Harness-->>Model: ERROR + error lines only
    end
    opt study one region close up
      Model->>Harness: look({ view }) or look({ at })
      Harness->>Renderer: render the one framed region
      Renderer-->>Harness: 1400px close-up
      Harness-->>Model: close-up + MEASURES + BOARD + BOARD DIFF + DIAGNOSTICS + ROUTES + REQUESTS
    end
  end
  opt dispose each user request
    Model->>Harness: resolve_request(id, status, note)
    Harness-->>Model: updated REQUESTS queue
  end
  Model->>Harness: finalize(committed, message)
  Harness->>Harness: run the scoped finding gate, check requests, diff baseline to draft
  alt any scoped finding or open request remains
    Harness-->>Model: blocked; run continues
  else gates pass
    Harness-->>Studio: proposal-ready(cumulative patch)
    Studio-->>Studio: operator reviews the proposed board change
  end
Reading the diagram
The operator defines the task and its starting scope.

The selection expands through selected sections to their descendants. The harness records the resulting object ids, scope frame, and boundary-connection count, then creates a draft. A frameless document receives a locked background page frame in the draft.
The model boots with current perception.

Five blocks arrive in order: editor_state, user_requests, capabilities, style_guide, and board_state. Nested XML children are indented four spaces. The capabilities block comes in two halves: first the material (sections, stickies, objects, and connections, each with its description, named functionality, and tips, while objects adds generated vocabulary and connections adds generated fields) and then one gestures block, a child per verb group, naming each tool and what it does to the board. A kind block says what the thing is and names no tools. The gesture half is read off the registration roster, so it cannot drift from the surface. The style guide carries one nested aesthetic topic: “Calm and uniform: uniformity is information.” It treats matched size and gap as a peer signal, sizes content first, repeats one gap per group, uses the 20 grid only for quantization, leaves air, groups through sections, reserves red for failure and green for success, and labels edges directly. board_state supplies the full digest and diagnostics. The image hook adds the current full-board render first, the house exemplar second, and the vocabulary contact sheet third. The sheet renders every type, icon glyph, and color plus connection demonstrations, including a wire ending on a section.
The model studies first, then edits through typed tools.

Twenty-five typed mutators are factored by editing gesture rather than by kind (place, arrange, content, sections, edges, delete), and each call is one gesture. look is the read-only inspection tool. Creation is per-kind and carries only what the UI's creation gesture carries, so a placement is a bare payload and everything else about the placed object comes from defaults. The exceptions travel with the name: place_shape and place_section may carry the one-line detail, and place_section may also carry a header icon for the section's title chip. The closed shape-and-icon type roster folds icon glyphs in under their own names. The roster intentionally gives bare type names, with icon glyphs and colors enumerated one per line, and geometry the agent writes lands on its own 20 grid.
The harness applies mechanics and pushes truth back.

After every operation, section membership and connection waypoints are both reconciled from geometry. Sections hold exactly the geometry they are given and close around their children only when fit_section names them. Ancestors keep their slack until named too. An applied operation returns its APPLIED line, any notes, the document-derived DELTA exposing snapped geometry, reconciled parentId and anchor, endpoint-position, or waypoint steering changes, the lint delta, and ROUTES for any connection it touched. Every edge gesture returns that edge's fresh numbered polyline, including on a no-op, so a second routing call in the same turn chains off the result rather than off a stale digest. A no-op returns its note, and an error returns its error lines. Neither changes the draft. Every draft write goes through one commit choke point that assigns the draft and captures fresh pixels in the same move, so the state block on the next turn carries the board as it now stands together with the digest, the cumulative diff, the findings, and the queue. An edit takes no view argument and returns no picture: framing is look's alone, and one call frames one region (view for a section or a single object, at for a world rect), returning it rendered and measured beside that same standing text. Lints explain what is wrong in prose. The model chooses the fix.
The model disposes requests and finalizes.

resolve_request marks one queue entry done or declined, records a note for the operator, and returns only the updated queue. finalize with outcome committed reruns diagnostics in the edited scope, requires every finding there to be cleared (warnings block exactly as errors do) and no user request left open, and proposes the cumulative baseline-to-draft patch. A blocked finalize leaves the run going, so the model fixes what it raised and calls again. outcome none ends without a proposal and explains why.

props.title: The handoff is a cumulative patch

text.insert: The model works on a session draft. BOARD DIFF is rendered from the same internal baseline-to-draft operations that a successful finalize proposes, so the operator reviews the change the model has been seeing throughout the run.

There are exactly thirty-two tools, factored by editing gesture rather than by kind: twenty-five board mutators across place, arrange, content, sections, edges, and delete; plus look, add_annotation, reply_annotation, resolve_request, update_description, set_board_title, and finalize. The full roster is below. The system prompt has four top-level sections: purpose, board_model, state_grammar, and workflow. There is no separate rules section; required behavior lives in phase constraints. workflow organizes work into five state-driven phases: orientate, plan, build, qa, and finalize, with each phase carrying its objective, steps, and constraints. Build places the section skeleton first, fills one section at a time while judging a render, closes each finished region with fit_section, then adds connections, labels, and styling. QA judges the whole board from the render attached to the state block and each touched section from a framed look, and finalize disposes requests and resolves diagnostics.
Key facts
Perception is deliberate.

The standing picture arrives on its own: every turn's state block carries the board digest, the cumulative change, the complete lints, routed truth, the request queue, and a render of the board as it stands, followed by up to three prior post-change renders. The digest is an indented containment tree followed by one EDGES block. Its legend declares elided defaults, and object text is never truncated. An object line's extras open with
icon=<glyph>
for a section's header icon and
detail="…"

for a detail line, each printed only when set. look is the deliberate close-up layered on that. It frames exactly one region per call, with view taking a section or a single object and at cropping to a world rect, either/or and never both. The framed region comes back both rendered and measured: per-pair gaps on each axis, row and column pitch, the section's free margins, and ink share. Conformance is therefore read rather than computed. Operation results stay focused on what they touched and carry no render at all.
Operations are semantic at the boundary and mechanical underneath.

The model writes twenty-five editing gestures. They lower to the six object-and-connection patch kinds used by the draft applier, document differ, and studio proposal wire. Geometry the model writes snaps to its own 20 grid before lowering, and parentId supplied by the model is not authoritative because containment is reconciled from placement.
The camera frames what is painted.

renderBoardView measures object rectangles, routed polylines, connection-label chips, zoom-scaled section-title chips, and icon captions, then adds padding. renderSectionView retains every painted item intersecting its camera; boundary-crossing connections remain visible to the frame edge and are clipped there rather than dropped.
Diagnostics measure legibility, and the model judges composition.

Eight always-on diagnostics run at spawn and on every edit. Six check covered content, containment, broken edges, unreadable labels, crowding, and clipped text against production geometry. The other two, label-is-prose and detail-too-long, hold object text to the name and detail convention. A shape, icon, or section name stays a few words on one line, its detail holds one short fact, and prose goes on a sticky. A committed finalize adds frame-slack, a polish check that would only nag while a region is still being built. Clipped text fires when a shape label, sticky body, or section title would drop words behind an ellipsis, or a detail line would be cut short or hidden. It names the measured box size that shows the text whole. Crowding is a warning-tier arrow-corridor floor: it flags sibling gaps under 80px side by side or 48px stacked, the clearance a routed wire and its chip physically need rather than a preferred distance. Every finding in the edited scope blocks a committed finalize, warnings included: the call is refused, the run continues, and the model fixes what it raised before calling again.
Factored by gesture
The agent's complete tool surface (every board-mutating gesture plus the perception, annotation, and run-lifecycle calls) is factored by
editing gesture

rather than by CRUD per kind. Each tool is one thing a person does in one motion on the real canvas: place a thing, move it, resize it, retitle it, slide a connector segment out of the way. Two consequences fall out of that framing.
The tool list is the capability matrix.
"Can a section's border change?" is answered by
change_section_border
existing and its schema naming its target kind, not by prose inside a catch-all patch.
Required parameters are structural.
Every verb's schema states exactly what that gesture needs. There are no everything-optional patches.

props.title: A trace reads like an editing session

text.insert: A run's tool calls read as
place, place, connect, move_by, resize, change_color
, the sequence a person would perform, in the order they would perform it. That is what the playback rail animates and what the eval judges read.
The roster
The surface is thirty-two tools: twenty-five board-mutating gestures in six groups, listed by
operationTools
, plus seven workflow calls listed by
workflowTools
. Those two arrays are the single source the agent catalog registers from and the
<capabilities>
block derives from, so a tool defined in a group module is not on the surface until it is listed there. The table below is their registration order, which is roughly the order a board gets built;
test/tool-schema-parity.test.ts
pins the roster and the structural invariants every schema satisfies.

rows: draw a titled frame that adopts whatever its edges already cover, with an optional header icon and one-fact detail
drop a note with its text already on it
the pick and the click: an untitled shape or glyph at its default size, with an optional one-fact detail
copy one object's kind, size, and look onto a new id, its detail line and glyph included
route an edge between two objects
put a box's top-left corner at a point on the board
nudge a box by an offset from where it already is
re-size a box to explicit dimensions, holding its top-left corner
copy another box's width and height onto this one
put a row or column of boxes on one shared edge or centerline
re-pitch a run so the clear gap between neighbours is exactly what you ask for
write a name and its one-line detail, a sticky's body, or an edge's label
recolor anything that carries a color, edges included
swap what a shape is and which way it points, or set a section's header icon
close a section around the children already inside it
protect a region, either the frame alone or the frame and everything in it
redraw an edge's line and arrowheads
repoint one end of an edge, leaving both endpoint objects unchanged
replace an edge's interior corners wholesale
slide one numbered segment of the route sideways
hand an edge back to the auto-router
pin the label chip along the routed path
remove one thing, with the cascade its kind implies
study one framed region close up, rendered and measured
replace the board's standing account wholesale
anchor a question to one object as a thread the user answers later
post a reply into a thread without moving its status
dispose one open request as done or declined, with a note
end the run, with a proposal or without one
props.title: Thirty-two tools, in registration order

text.insert: Absorbed, not added
Three calls a gesture surface might be expected to carry are not tools, because an existing tool already answers what they would ask.
match_size
is the counterexample and is a real gesture on the roster: peer sizing is its own motion, and it earns its own verb.
measure
lives inside
look
's region readout. A framed region comes back rendered
and
measured (per-pair gaps on each axis, row and column pitch, the section's free margins, ink share), so conformance is read rather than computed in context.
distribute
is subsumed by
space_out
. Equalizing inside a fixed span can never open a gap, and the agent always knows its target gap from the craft targets, so the gesture that sets the pitch covers both jobs.
route_around
is not on the surface. Route cleanup is deliberate elbow work (
shift_segment
for one segment,
reroute
for the whole path), not a hint handed to a solver.
What the surface excludes
Three capabilities sit outside the surface's scope. Each is buildable from what is on the roster, and each has a condition under which it is worth revisiting.
Multi-id variants
of
move_to
move_by
change_color
, and
delete
(the UI's selection grammar). Batching would speed a run but cuts against one gesture, one operation. The two multi-id gestures that do exist,
align
and
space_out
, take a list because the arrangement itself is the gesture. Revisit once single-id traces show where batching earns its keep.
A quick-connect gesture
, an
extend(fromId, id, direction, text?)
that drops a blank same-styled copy one half-width away, already wired, in one history entry. The surface builds the same result as a
clone
followed by a
connect
Annotation-targeted creation and deletion.
add_annotation
anchors a thread to exactly one object (there are no intent or region targets), and
delete
takes board ids only, never an annotation id. A thread is disposed with
resolve_request
, not removed.

A capability the roster does not name is a capability the agent does not have. There is no escape hatch tool, no raw patch, and no free-form document write: the twenty-five gestures are the only way the draft changes.
Two hosts, one surface

The roster is defined once and reaches a board through one runtime binding, and two hosts supply the session behind that binding. The kernel host runs the edit this page opens with: a scoped draft, a model run, and a proposal the operator accepts. The file host opens a
canvases/<id>.canvas.json
file directly as a session in
packages/canvas-agent/src/toolkit/index.ts

, with no kernel and no model process, and serves the tools to an external agent over MCP. Tool names, descriptions, schemas, and validation are identical on both hosts. The lifecycle around the tools differs in four ways.
The file host carries thirty-one of the thirty-two tools.
finalize
is absent because a file session has no run to end and no proposal to commit.
The file host has no operator selection, so its scope is the whole board.
The file host saves every applied edit at once. The diff since the last save replays onto the file through
canvas.applyAgentPatch

, the reducer action an accepted proposal dispatches, so both hosts leave the same document. The save is refused when the file changed on disk since the session last read or wrote it, and the caller reopens the canvas.
The file host pushes no boot context and no state block. The caller receives the board description, digest, and lint report when it opens the canvas, and calls
look
for a render.
